hints: Look at the value of $R$ when $V=0$ on each graph - should a cold metal filament have zero resistance or a finite resistance?
Recall that power $P = IV = V^2/R$ heats the filament, so increasing $V$ raises the metal temperature toward normal brightness.
Connect higher metal temperature to more lattice vibration and more electron collisions, so decide whether $R$ should stay constant, fall or rise with $V$.
walkthrough: Identify what is plotted: resistance $R = V/I$ on the vertical axis against applied p.d. $V$ on the horizontal axis, from $V=0$ up to normal brightness.
State the physics: current heats the filament by $P = IV$. As $V$ increases, the filament temperature rises sharply.
For a metal, higher temperature means larger resistivity because vibrating ions scatter conduction electrons more, so $R$ increases with $V$.
At $V=0$ there is no heating but the cold filament is still a metal wire, so $R$ must start at a positive finite value, not at zero.
Only a graph that starts above the origin and slopes upward matches a steadily increasing $R$ with $V$. This is option A.

A.explanation: Starts at a non-zero cold resistance at $V=0$ and $R$ rises as $V$ increases due to heating of the filament.

B.explanation: Shows $R=0$ at $V=0$, but a metal filament has a finite cold resistance even before heating.

C.explanation: Shows constant $R$, which is ohmic behaviour and ignores the temperature rise of the filament with increasing $V$.

D.explanation: Shows $R$ falling with $V$, which is opposite to a filament and more like an NTC thermistor.
